note: The six glyph properties and their four states (RFC-0016). Our words are in reason, note, rules and not_here; quote text is the system's (or RFC-0015's) own. Nothing here adds, counts or orders states.

properties.name: Weights hidden
properties.not_here: Hiding the weights from the host operator (an enclave) is not this property.
properties.question: Does the checker learn nothing about the weights?

rules.no: The documentation says the checker sees the weights, or that hiding is off or not provided.
rules.not_stated: No statement about hiding the weights from the checker in the sources read, or not copied yet.
rules.partly: The documentation says they are hidden with a stated limit: a named leak, hiding shown for one policy or setting only, hiding optional per circuit, or hiding behind a commitment without the formal zero-knowledge property.
rules.yes: The documentation says the weights stay hidden from the checker in the default use, naming no leak beyond public settings.

properties.name: Model bound
properties.not_here: Which real, named model the commitment is: FlashProve and SASH both say that stays outside their proof; it does not change the state.
properties.question: Is each checked token tied to the committed weights?

rules.no: The documentation says outputs are not tied to any weights, or that nothing is checked.
rules.not_stated: Not stated in the sources read, or not copied yet.
rules.partly: Tied with a stated limit: under one of several policies only, within a tolerance or bound, or shown only in empirical tests.
rules.yes: The documentation says a passing check ties each checked token to the committed weights exactly, in the configuration the row reads.

properties.name: Whole output checked
properties.not_here: Which requests get a check (sampling, proving after the fact) is a deployment choice, not what one check covers. The text before tokenizing and after detokenizing, which FlashProve and SASH both put outside their proof, does not change the state.
properties.question: Does one check cover every output token of a request?

rules.no: The documentation says no output token is checked, or that nothing is checked.
rules.not_stated: Not stated, including a proved run whose output tokens the documentation does not name, or not copied yet.
rules.partly: One check covers a stated part: the positions the client names, one segment, or one disputed step.
rules.yes: The documentation says one check, or one joined set of checks, covers the prompt and every output token of a request.

properties.name: Formally verified
properties.not_here: A proof that the code itself is correct: no row claims it. A statement made only for another configuration of the same system, another verifier for one, sets nothing here.
properties.question: Is the security argument for the row's configuration checked by a proof assistant?

rules.no: The documentation says the argument is not machine-checked, that a machine check is planned only, or that its soundness evidence is review or tests and nothing else; or the row is a reference, which has no security argument by definition.
rules.not_stated: Not stated in the sources read, or not copied yet.
rules.partly: Machine-checked for a stated part only: one component, or a weaker statement than the one the system makes.
rules.yes: The documentation says the soundness of the configuration the row reads is proved in a proof assistant (Lean, Coq, Isabelle or similar).

properties.name: Security level
properties.not_here: The level itself: the state shows only whether one is stated and proven. A level stated only for another configuration of the same system sets nothing here.
properties.question: Is a soundness level stated for the row's configuration, and proven?

rules.no: The documentation says the settings give no meaningful soundness, for example a test-only setting; or the row is a reference, which has no soundness level by definition.
rules.not_stated: No level stated for the configuration in the sources read, or not copied yet.
rules.partly: A numeric level is stated but called conjectured, or stated only in code or configuration, or for part of the system.
rules.yes: The documentation states a numeric soundness bound for the configuration the row reads and says it is proven, by hand or by machine, under named assumptions.

properties.name: No trusted party
properties.not_here: Trust every row shares does not change the state: the checker's own computer, compiler and verifier build, and where the commitment or the weights come from (see Model bound).
properties.question: Does a check hold without trusting a chip maker, a setup ceremony or an honest party?

rules.no: The documentation says the check verifies a hardware attestation against a chip maker's keys or certificate chain, or that the provider is trusted. Running in a trusted execution environment, said alone, is not such a statement.
rules.not_stated: Not stated in the sources read, or not copied yet.
rules.partly: The documentation states a trusted input or condition that its proved statement does not cover: a setup file, public files the user must grant were fixed before the hash, or one honest party among several.
rules.yes: The documentation says the check rests on cryptography alone or needs no trusted setup, and names no chip maker, setup or other party to trust.

formally_verified.note: Searched for: machine-checked, machine checked, formal, Lean, Coq, audit, human review, soundness. docs/statement.md argues each edge in prose; no passage says how that argument is checked.

stwo's own conjectured-soundness accounting is

security_level.reason: Level stated as conjectured, in a source code comment.

weights_hidden.note: Our note: no passage says whether a proof hides the weights. Two passages come near and were not copied into this slot because neither states it: the verifier compares the model root with a published manifest because "it commits weights the verifier does not hold" (zk-inference-prover docs/decisions/2026-09-09-the-verifier-derives-the-shape-root.md L10-L12), and the model's shape is "things the verifier knows rather than things the proof hides" (zk-inference-results docs/statement-gap.md L172-L175).

whole_output.note: The request is checked as a grid of segment proofs joined by boundary-grid; the benchmark counts the grid as one proof (systems/sash/README.md).

quotes.label: docs/statement-gap.md L3-L7 · 11decec3
quotes.text: The prover proves one end-to-end statement about one request: every position of a prompt and of a 512-token greedy continuation, from the embedding up through every layer and through the output head

outside_pin.reason: One end-to-end statement about one request, in the companion results repository.

quotes.label: prover/src/boundary.rs L1148-L1153 · eb95bfa8
quotes.text: The token axis of the *sequence* -- as distinct from the K/V axis of the grid -- is checked here too, and unconditionally: every position of every block whose layer-0 chunk carries the embedding gadget is either a prompt position, whose id must equal the prompt's, or a generated one, whose id must equal the token the `lm_head` chunk proved for the position before it (within a block, and across the block seam at `t = 0`).

quotes.label: docs/statement.md L5-L7 · eb95bfa8
quotes.text: A sequence is proved as a grid of such segments, and `boundary-grid` checks that the segments fit together.

whole_output.reason: Every prompt and generated position is checked across the joined grid of segment proofs.

no.meaning: The documentation says it does not hold, by the property's No rule; or it says it holds, fully or partly, and a negative control of the benchmark contradicts it.

not_stated.meaning: The sources read say nothing that meets the Yes, Partly or No rule, or they have not been read yet. Silence is never No.

partly.meaning: The documentation says it holds with a limit it states, by the property's Partly rule, and no control of the benchmark contradicts it.

yes.meaning: The documentation says the property holds, by the property's Yes rule, and no control of the benchmark contradicts it.
